title: The boy who asked what dies
hookLine: a sixteen-year-old in Madurai lies down on the floor and acts out his own death
carry: who am i? the self, not the body
tomorrow: karma: seva, and a word Ramakrishna refused
last: IN BHAKTI, LOVE RUNS BOTH WAYS: SOMETIMES GOD BOWS.

cards: Madurai, South India, the summer of 1896. A sixteen-year-old boy named Venkataraman is alone in a room in his uncle's house. He's healthy.
Nothing is wrong. Suddenly an overwhelming fear hits him: he's about to die. He could call someone, or go for a walk.
He does something else. He lies down on the floor, stretches out his limbs like a corpse, holds his breath, and says to himself: all right. Death has come.
What does it mean? What is it that's dying?

teach.h: THE BODY DIES. AM I DEAD?
teach.b: Lying there, as he later told it, he reasoned it through. This body is dead. They'll carry it to the cremation ground and burn it.
But with the body dead, am I dead? Is the body I? And in that moment, he said, he knew directly that he was not the body.
The fear vanished and never came back. He hadn't studied any of this, he said later, but Hindus have an old name for what he found: the atman, the Self.

teach.h: THE ATMAN: NOT BORN, NOT DYING.
teach.b: The Gita puts it plainly: the body is born and dies; the Self is not born and does not die.
A few weeks later he left home with a short note and took a train toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, in the town of Tiruvannamalai. He stayed there more than fifty years.
People came to call him Ramana Maharshi, and they came from far away just to sit with him.
When he did teach, the heart of it was one question: who am I? Not I'm a student, I'm a parent, I'm tired. Those are things you have, he'd say, in effect, not what you are.
Follow the feeling of I back to where it comes from.

That's self-inquiry: the jnana road with almost nothing extra. So when the world sums you up in one label, the grade, the job, the mistake, this is the Hindu answer: the atman isn't any of those. Ask who am I, and look.

how: Visitors to Ramana Maharshi's ashram at Tiruvannamalai sit in silence in his old hall and walk around the hill of Arunachala; followers practice self-inquiry by turning attention to the sense of I rather than to its thoughts.

o: a vow of silence kept until you are free
a name given to you by your teacher
action, even turning to look at who you are

p: he lay down and acted out death
following I back to its source
the Self the body's death can't touch

s: Ramana's turning point came after years of study with a guru
it came suddenly, at sixteen, alone on the floor of his uncle's house.
Ramana stayed at Arunachala for the rest of his life
more than fifty years, at the mountain in Tiruvannamalai.
Ramana found that he was his body, so death was the end of him
he found the opposite: he was not the body. Hindus call that Self the atman.

games.q: you're sixteen, healthy, and suddenly overwhelmed by the fear that you're about to die. what did Ramana do?
o: lay down like a corpse and asked what dies.
games.why: he acted out his own death and asked: with the body dead, am I dead? the fear vanished and never came back.

practice: Ask the question once, quietly: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a role; just notice the plain sense of being here, this I that's listening, and when a thought comes, let it pass and come back to the question.
Rest in the space where the answer would be; it's fine if nothing happens, because the looking is the practice, and if you pray, you can rest in God as the source of that I.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action was to lie down and look, and he spent his life inviting others to look too.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ko'ham, 'who am I?'. Ramana's short Tamil teaching text asks the same question in its title, Nan Yar?

carryVoice: Your line: who am I? The Self, not the body. Not a name, not a label: the one asking. See you tomorrow.
